fractions.title: Make sense of the fraction
opening: A fraction is a division, even when the top contains several terms. Read the whole top (the numerator) as one quantity and the whole bottom (the denominator) as another. In a rate, the bottom often tells you the time interval you are dividing by.
I’ll do a numerical division first, then the algebraic one that appears in the derivative lesson. The same principle applies: divide the entire numerator.

examples.title: A small time interval can give a large rate
examples.setup: An object moves 6 metres in 0.2 seconds. Find its average speed.

steps.title: Write what is being shared
steps.why: We are finding metres for each one second. Since 0.2 seconds is only one fifth of a second, a one-second interval contains five intervals of this length.

steps.title: Clear the decimal without changing the ratio
steps.why: Multiplying top and bottom by the same nonzero number leaves the fraction unchanged. Multiplying only the bottom would change the question.

steps.title: Put the unit back
steps.why: Check backwards: 30 m/s × 0.2 s = 6 m. The seconds cancel and the distance returns. A smaller divisor can produce a larger answer; division does not always make a number smaller.

examples.answer: The average speed is 30 m/s. We have made no claim that the speed was constant inside the interval.

examples.title: Simplify the fraction used in a derivative

steps.title: Keep both terms over the denominator
steps.why: Both terms are divided by h. Do not cancel a symbol from only one term and leave the other untouched.

steps.title: Divide out a common factor
steps.why: Equivalently, factor the entire top: h(6 + h)/h. A common nonzero factor multiplying the entire top and bottom can be divided out.

steps.title: Keep the condition
steps.why: The original expression is undefined at h = 0. In a derivative calculation we simplify at nonzero h, then ask what happens as h approaches zero. We do not repair division by zero by pretending it was allowed.

examples.answer: At h = 0.1 the value is 6.1; at h = −0.1 it is 5.9. Both approach 6 as h approaches zero.

fractions.remember: Cancel common factors, not pieces joined by addition. Keep any conditions that made the division valid.

equations.title: Keep the equation balanced
opening: An equation says two amounts are equal. I can change its appearance if I do the same allowed operation to both sides. The goal is to leave the unknown by itself without changing which values make the statement true.
Instead of saying “move the 3 across,” I’ll name the operation. That makes the sign and the division easier to check.

examples.title: Find the speed after a sticking collision
examples.setup: The total mass is 3 kg and the horizontal momentum is +8 kg·m/s. Solve 3v = 8 using those units.

steps.title: Identify the multiplication
steps.why: The 3 multiplies v. To undo multiplication by 3 kg, divide both sides by 3 kg.

steps.title: Apply the same division
steps.why: On the left, the mass factor becomes one. On the right, kilograms cancel, leaving a velocity unit.

steps.title: Leave an exact answer, then check it
steps.why: Use the fraction in later energy calculations so rounding does not accumulate. Checking with the fraction gives (3 kg)(8/3 m/s) = 8 kg·m/s exactly.

examples.answer: The shared velocity is +8/3 m/s. The positive sign means motion in the direction we chose as positive.

examples.title: Undo addition before multiplication

steps.title: Remove the added 10
steps.why: Subtract 10 from both sides. The left becomes −2t; the right becomes −6.

steps.title: Undo multiplication by −2
steps.why: The multiplier includes its minus sign. Dividing only by +2 would leave −t, not t.

steps.title: Substitute into the original statement
steps.why: Checking the original equation catches mistakes that can hide in a chain of algebra. If t is time in a model valid only for 0–4 minutes, 3 is also within the allowed interval.

examples.answer: t = 3 satisfies the equation and the stated time interval.

equations.remember: Name the operation on both sides. Check your answer in the original equation, with units and the model’s allowed values.

squares.title: Squares, square roots and exact fractions
opening: Squaring means multiplying a number by itself. A square root reverses that operation for a nonnegative number. These look like small symbols, but missing either one can change a physics answer substantially.
I’ll keep fractions exact for the calculation, then round the final measured quantity. I’ll also separate a mathematical solution from a physical choice of sign.

examples.title: Square the whole velocity
examples.setup: Three kilograms move at 8/3 m/s. Find kinetic energy using KE = ½mv².

steps.title: Write the square as multiplication
steps.why: The denominator is squared too. The result is not 64/3, and it is not 16/3. Squaring a velocity also squares its unit: m²/s².

steps.title: Multiply the remaining factors
steps.why: One way to simplify is 3/9 = 1/3 first, then (1/2)(64/3) = 32/3. Both routes give the same fraction.

steps.title: Round after the energy calculation
steps.why: The unit kg·m²/s² is a joule. If you first round the speed to 2.67, the final result changes slightly. Keeping 8/3 avoids that rounding error.

examples.answer: The kinetic energy is exactly 32/3 J in this ideal model.

examples.title: Take the square root after isolating x²
examples.setup: A spring calculation gives 24x² = 32/3, with x measured in metres. Find the compression.

steps.title: Divide to isolate the square
steps.why: The 24 multiplies the entire x². Dividing both sides by it leaves a square, not yet x.

steps.title: Find both algebraic solutions
steps.why: Both +2/3 and −2/3 square to 4/9. The symbol √(4/9) alone means the nonnegative root; solving x² = 4/9 requires considering both signs.

steps.title: Use the meaning of the variable
steps.why: Here x was defined as a nonnegative amount of compression, so we choose +2/3. If x were a signed displacement coordinate, we would inspect the physical direction before choosing a sign.

squares.remember: Square the whole fraction. Isolate the square before taking a root. Choose a sign from what the variable means.

quadratic.title: Solve the quadratic without skipping the middle
opening: The tank reaches capacity when 3 + t² + t = 20. This has a squared unknown, so dividing by t would not isolate it. I’ll turn the left side into a single square, then take square roots.
This method is called completing the square. It also explains where the quadratic formula comes from, but you do not need to memorize that formula to follow this particular calculation.

examples.title: Find when the tank first holds 20 L
examples.setup: Solve 3 + t² + t = 20 for time t ≥ 0.

steps.title: Leave the variable terms together
steps.why: Subtract 3 from both sides. To make a square, use (t + a)² = t² + 2at + a². We want 2a = 1, so a = 1/2.

steps.title: Add the missing quarter to both sides
steps.why: Adding only to the left would change the equation. On the right, 17 = 68/4, so the sum is 69/4.

steps.title: Take roots, then subtract the half
steps.why: The plus choice gives about 3.653 minutes; the minus choice gives about −4.653 minutes. Our pump model starts at t = 0, so only the positive time answers this question.

examples.answer: The tank fills at (−1 + √69)/2 minutes. Substituting that root into 3 + t² + t returns 20 L.

examples.title: When factoring is quicker

steps.title: Find the two numbers
steps.why: Here the coefficient of x² is 1. We need two numbers with sum −5 and product +6 to expand (x − 2)(x − 3).

steps.title: Check the multiplication
steps.why: Write all four products so the signs remain visible. The two middle terms combine to −5x.

steps.title: Use the zero product
steps.why: A product of real numbers is zero only when at least one factor is zero. This argument needs the right side to be zero; it would not justify setting each factor to zero if the product equaled 10.

examples.answer: Both 2 and 3 satisfy the original equation. A physical problem might allow both, one or neither depending on its domain.

quadratic.remember: Some quadratics factor neatly; others do not. Keep both roots until the problem’s meaning rules one out.

graphs.title: Read the axes before reading the shape
opening: A rising line does not always mean an object is speeding up. First ask what the vertical axis measures. The slope of a position graph measures velocity; the area under a velocity graph measures displacement.
I’ll use the same three seconds in two different graphs. The units will tell us which calculation makes sense.

examples.title: Use rise over run on a position graph
examples.setup: Position is s(t) = t² metres. Find the average velocity from t = 1 s to t = 3 s.

steps.title: Read the endpoints as coordinate pairs
steps.line: Start: (1 s, 1 m). Finish: (3 s, 9 m).
steps.why: The horizontal change is 3 − 1 = 2 s. The vertical change is 9 − 1 = 8 m. Pair each position with the time at which it occurs.

steps.title: Divide the two changes
steps.why: This is the slope of the straight line joining the endpoints, called a secant. It summarizes the interval, even though the curve itself bends.

steps.title: Separate the interval rate from an instant
steps.line: Instantaneous velocity here is s′(t) = 2t, so at 3 s it is 6 m/s.
steps.why: The interval average is 4 m/s and the final instantaneous value is 6 m/s. Both are correct answers to different questions. The steeper curve near the finish agrees with the larger final velocity.

examples.answer: Position-graph slope has units metres per second.

examples.title: Use area on a velocity graph
examples.setup: Velocity is v(t) = 2t m/s. Find displacement from t = 1 s to t = 3 s.

steps.title: Read the heights and the width
steps.line: v(1) = 2 m/s; v(3) = 6 m/s; width = 2 s
steps.why: The straight velocity line forms a trapezoid above the time axis over this interval.

steps.title: Find the area
steps.why: The average height is 4 m/s and the width is 2 s. Multiplying gives 8 m. A thin strip follows the same unit rule: velocity times a short time gives a small displacement.

steps.title: Check against the position formula
steps.why: The result agrees with the first graph’s change in position. In this positive-velocity interval, displacement and distance traveled have the same value; that would need more care if velocity changed sign.

examples.answer: Velocity-graph area has units metres. Its slope would instead have acceleration units, m/s².

graphs.remember: Slope divides vertical change by horizontal change. Area multiplies vertical and horizontal units. Name the axes first.

signs.title: Keep the signs and units attached
opening: A minus sign can describe a direction, not a mistake. Choose a positive direction once, then give every velocity its sign before adding momenta or calculating a change.
Units are part of the calculation too. They can tell you that you found an acceleration when the question asked for a velocity, even if the numerical arithmetic looks tidy.

examples.title: Add momenta from opposite directions
examples.setup: A 2 kg cart moves right at 3 m/s. A 1 kg cart moves left at 3 m/s. They stick. Choose right as positive.

steps.title: Write the velocities with signs
steps.why: The speeds are equal, but the velocities are opposite. The first cart also has twice the mass, so we should expect a remaining rightward momentum.

steps.title: Add the signed momenta
steps.why: Adding the speeds would lose the direction information. The total mass after sticking is 3 kg, so the shared velocity is +3/3 = +1 m/s.

steps.title: Check the direction and the energy
steps.why: Squaring a negative velocity gives a positive number. Kinetic energy has no left/right sign. The reduction is 12 J in this sticking model, while total momentum remains +3 kg·m/s during the brief collision.

examples.answer: The joined carts move right at 1 m/s. Opposite momenta can partially cancel; positive kinetic energies do not cancel that way.

examples.title: Read the two “per seconds” in acceleration
examples.setup: Velocity changes from +2 m/s to +8 m/s in 3 s. Find average acceleration.

steps.title: Subtract in the same order
steps.why: Use the chosen positive direction throughout. The change is positive because the velocity became more positive.

steps.title: Divide by elapsed time
steps.why: One second comes from the velocity unit and another from dividing by the elapsed time. The answer is a change of 2 m/s for each second, on average over this interval.

steps.title: Check the dimensions of a prediction
steps.why: Multiplying acceleration by time returns the velocity change when the stated acceleration is constant. Over an arbitrary varying acceleration, the interval average still reproduces the total change over that interval.

examples.answer: Acceleration has units m/s²; it is not a distance and not a velocity.

signs.remember: Choose a direction, keep the signs, and carry units through the same operations as the numbers.

powers.title: Differentiate and accumulate, one term at a time
opening: A position or volume formula describes an amount. Its derivative describes the rate at which that amount changes. An integral of a rate adds up the changes; an initial condition tells you where the amount started.
I’ll show the small power rules used in the course, then check the result by going back the other way. These examples use simple terms such as t², t and a constant.

examples.title: Differentiate a polynomial without losing the constant rate

steps.title: Handle the squared term
steps.why: For these powers, bring the exponent down as a multiplier and reduce the exponent by one. The coefficient 3 remains a multiplier.

steps.title: Handle the linear and constant terms
steps.why: The 2t term adds 2 units of position for each extra unit of time, so its rate is a constant 2. The fixed position offset 5 adds no change as time passes.

steps.title: Put the term rates together
steps.why: A derivative can contain a constant. What disappears is a constant amount in the original function, not every constant-looking number in the result.

examples.answer: At t = 2, the instantaneous rate is 6(2) + 2 = 14. The position there is 21; amount and rate remain different quantities.

examples.title: Accumulate a flow and restore the initial volume
examples.setup: The rate is r(t) = 2t + 1 L/min; the tank starts at 3 L. Find its unrestricted volume at t = 2 min.

steps.title: Find a function with the needed derivative
steps.why: We reverse the two polynomial rules: integrating 2t gives t², and integrating 1 gives t. An added constant would not affect the derivative.

steps.title: Evaluate the accumulation between endpoints
steps.why: The integral gives water added during the interval. The temporary variable u keeps the integration step separate from its upper limit.

steps.title: Add the starting amount
steps.why: A derivative alone cannot tell whether the tank began empty or with 3 L. The starting condition supplies the missing constant. Capacity and overflow must then be checked separately if the tank is small enough to fill.

examples.answer: The unrestricted formula is W(t) = 3 + t² + t. It satisfies both W(0) = 3 and W′(t) = 2t + 1.

powers.remember: Check an accumulated formula in two ways: differentiate it to recover the rate, then test its value at the starting time.
